tagline: A beach for every day of the year
overview:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small nation of two main islands in the eastern Caribbean, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Caribbean Sea. Antigua, the larger and busier island, is home to the capital, Saint John's, and nearly all of the country's roughly 100,000 people. Barbuda, about 40 kilometers to the north, is flat, quiet and ringed with pink-tinged sand. A third island, rocky Redonda, has no people at all. Together they cover just 442 km², smaller than many cities.

Islanders like to say Antigua has 365 beaches, one for every day of the year. Tourism is the biggest business, along with sailing, fishing and banking. Cruise ships dock in Saint John's beneath the white towers of the cathedral.

The country is an independent member of the Commonwealth. It has its own parliament and prime minister, while the British monarch remains head of state. English is the official language, and most people also speak a lively Antiguan Creole.
landAndNature:
Antigua is made mostly of limestone and old volcanic rock, with low rolling hills that rise to Boggy Peak, about 400 meters high. Because there are few rivers, the island can suffer droughts, and coral reefs sit close to shore in shallow, turquoise water. Barbuda is even lower and flatter, a coral island with a huge lagoon on its western side.

The climate is warm all year, with a rainy season from June to November that is also hurricane season; Hurricane Irma badly damaged Barbuda in 2017. Codrington Lagoon on Barbuda shelters one of the world's largest colonies of magnificent frigatebirds, whose males puff up bright red throat pouches. Hawksbill turtles nest on the beaches, and the rare Antiguan racer snake survives on tiny offshore islands.
peopleAndCulture:
Most Antiguans and Barbudans are descended from Africans brought to the islands to work on sugar plantations. English is the official language, and the local Creole is spoken at home and in songs. The national dish is fungee, a cornmeal and okra paste, served with pepperpot stew; ducana, a sweet potato dumpling, and saltfish are other favorites.

Cricket is close to a religion here. Antigua produced Sir Vivian Richards, one of the greatest batsmen ever, and the national stadium is named after him. Sailing is the other passion: Antigua Sailing Week draws yachts from around the world each spring. Carnival, held from late July into early August, celebrates the end of slavery with steel bands, calypso and soca music, and dancers in feathered costumes.
history:
The first people, ancestors of the Arawak and later the Kalinago, reached the islands more than 2,000 years ago, fishing and farming cassava. Christopher Columbus sailed past in 1493 and named Antigua after a church in Seville, Spain. English settlers arrived in 1632 and cut down the forests to plant sugarcane.

For two centuries, enslaved Africans did the brutal work of the plantations, and the harbor at English Harbour became a base for the British navy. Slavery was abolished in 1834, and formerly enslaved people built free villages across the island. Antigua remained a British colony until it gained full independence on November 1, 1981, with Barbuda as its partner. Since then the country has grown through tourism, and Nelson's Dockyard at English Harbour was named a World Heritage Site in 2016.
funFacts: Redonda, the country's uninhabited third island, was once mined for bird droppings, which were sold as fertilizer.
The magnificent frigatebird colony in Barbuda's Codrington Lagoon can hold several thousand birds at nesting time.
Antigua's highest hill was officially called Mount Obama from 2009 to 2016, then given back its old name, Boggy Peak.
The Antiguan racer was once called the world's rarest snake, with only about 50 left; conservation has raised the number to more than 1,000.
Barbuda's beaches look pink because they are mixed with crushed shells of tiny red sea creatures.
Nelson's Dockyard is the only working Georgian-era naval dockyard left in the world.
